notes.summary:
An index number measures the relative change in a group of related items (prices, quantities, wages) over time or between places, with the base period set at 100. Paper 2 asks 6 to 10 questions: simple and weighted indices, the Laspeyres, Paasche, Fisher and other formulas, tests of adequacy, chain-base indices, base shifting and splicing, and cost of living indices with real wages.

Index numbers are often called "economic barometers".

concepts.title: Meaning and notation
concepts.body:
• Base period: the reference period, index = 100. Current period: the period being compared.
  • p0, q0 = base-year price and quantity; p1, q1 = current-year price and quantity.
  • P01 = price index of year 1 with base year 0. Q01 = quantity index.
  • An index of 125 means a 25% rise over the base; 90 means a 10% fall.
  • Index numbers are specialised averages; they are expressed as percentages but written without the % sign.

concepts.title: Problems in constructing an index
concepts.body:
1. Purpose: decide exactly what the index will measure.
  2. Base year: a normal year, not too far back, free from wars, floods or booms.
  3. Choice of items: representative items, in standard qualities.
  4. Prices: wholesale or retail, from representative markets.
  5. Weights: show the relative importance of items (by quantity or by value).
  6. Average: the GM is theoretically best for relatives; the AM is used most often for ease.
  7. Formula: Laspeyres, Paasche, Fisher and so on.

concepts.title: Simple (unweighted) indices
concepts.body:
• Price relative = (p1 ÷ p0) × 100. Price ₹40 rises to ₹50: relative = 125.
  • Simple aggregative: P01 = (Σp1 ÷ Σp0) × 100. Easy, but items priced in bigger units dominate.
  • Simple average of relatives: P01 = Σ(p1/p0 × 100) ÷ n (AM), or the GM of the relatives.

Mini example: relatives 120, 150 and 90. Simple AM of relatives = 360 ÷ 3 = 120.

concepts.title: Weighted aggregative formulas
concepts.body:
NameWeightsPrice index P01 (× 100)
LaspeyresBase quantities q0Σp1q0 ÷ Σp0q0
PaascheCurrent quantities q1Σp1q1 ÷ Σp0q1
Fisher (ideal)Both√(Laspeyres × Paasche)
Marshall-Edgeworthq0 + q1Σp1(q0 + q1) ÷ Σp0(q0 + q1)
Dorbish-BowleyBoth(Laspeyres + Paasche) ÷ 2
Kelly (fixed weight)Fixed qΣp1q ÷ Σp0q
  • Laspeyres usually overstates price rise (upward bias); Paasche usually understates it (downward bias).
  • Fisher's index lies between them and is called "ideal".
  • Quantity indices swap p and q: Laspeyres Q01 = Σq1p0 ÷ Σq0p0 × 100.
  • Value index V01 = Σp1q1 ÷ Σp0q0 × 100.
  • Weighted average of relatives: Σ(PW) ÷ ΣW, where P = price relative and W = base value p0q0. With base values as weights it equals Laspeyres.

concepts.title: Worked example: Laspeyres, Paasche and Fisher
Tests of adequacy
concepts.body:
TestConditionSatisfied by
Unit testIndex does not depend on the units of prices or quantitiesAll except the simple aggregative index
Time reversal testP01 × P10 = 1 (without the 100s)Fisher, Marshall-Edgeworth, Kelly, simple aggregative, simple GM of relatives
Factor reversal testP01 × Q01 = Σp1q1 ÷ Σp0q0 (the value ratio)Fisher only (of the common formulas)
Circular testP01 × P12 × P20 = 1Simple GM of relatives, simple aggregative, Kelly (fixed weights); not Fisher

Fisher's index satisfies both the time reversal and factor reversal tests, so it is called the ideal index. Laspeyres and Paasche fail both.

concepts.title: Fixed base and chain base
concepts.body:
• Fixed base: every year is compared with one base year.
  • Link relative = (this year's price ÷ last year's price) × 100.
  • Chain index for a year = (link relative of the year × chain index of the previous year) ÷ 100. The first year's chain index is 100.
  • Chain base allows adding or dropping items easily and suits long periods, but an error in one link is carried forward.
  • For a single item, the chain index equals the fixed-base index.

Mini example: link relatives 110, 120, 90 for years 2, 3, 4. Chain indices: 110, 110 × 1.2 = 132, 132 × 0.9 = 118.8.

concepts.title: Base shifting, splicing and deflating
concepts.body:
• Base shifting: new index = (old index of the year ÷ old index of the new base year) × 100. If 2020 = 125 and 2023 = 150 on the old base, then on base 2020 the 2023 index is 150/125 × 100 = 120.
  • Splicing: joining an old series that ends at year k with a new series that starts at year k = 100. Forward splicing: multiply each new index by (old index of year k ÷ 100). Backward splicing: multiply each old index by (100 ÷ old index of year k).
  • Deflating: real value = (money value ÷ price index) × 100. Real wage of ₹30,000 at CPI 150 = ₹20,000.
  • Purchasing power of money = 100 ÷ price index (in base-year rupees). At CPI 125, ₹1 buys what ₹0.80 bought in the base year.

concepts.title: Cost of living (consumer price) index
concepts.body:
• Measures the change in the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by a given class of people (industrial workers, agricultural labourers, urban employees).
  • Main groups: food, clothing, fuel and light, house rent, miscellaneous.
  • Aggregate expenditure method: Σp1q0 ÷ Σp0q0 × 100 (Laspeyres).
  • Family budget method: ΣIW ÷ ΣW, where I = group index (or price relative) and W = weight (share of expenditure p0q0). Both methods give the same answer.
  • Uses: fixing dearness allowance, wage negotiation, deflating incomes, measuring purchasing power and inflation.
  • In India, CPI (Combined) by NSO is the headline inflation measure used by the RBI; WPI is compiled by the Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT).

Mini example: Food weight 50, index 120; Rent weight 20, index 150; Others weight 30, index 110. CLI = (6,000 + 3,000 + 3,300) ÷ 100 = 123.

concepts.title: Uses and limits
concepts.body:
• Uses: measure inflation, frame economic policy, adjust wages and DA, deflate national income, compare trends and places.
  • Limits: based on samples of items, quality changes are hard to capture, an index made for one purpose may mislead for another, and no single formula is perfect.

varieties.name: Simple price relatives and aggregative index
varieties.how: Price relative = p₁/p₀ × 100. Simple aggregative = Σp₁/Σp₀ × 100.

example.q: The price of a kilogram of rice was ₹40 in 2020 and ₹50 in 2025. Find the price index for 2025 with 2020 as base.

varieties.name: Laspeyres, Paasche, Fisher and others
varieties.how: Build four sums: Σp₀q₀, Σp₁q₀, Σp₀q₁, Σp₁q₁. Laspeyres uses q₀, Paasche uses q₁, Fisher is their GM.

example.q: A: p₀ = 2, q₀ = 10, p₁ = 3, q₁ = 12. B: p₀ = 5, q₀ = 4, p₁ = 6, q₁ = 5. Find Laspeyres' and Paasche's price indices.

varieties.name: Tests of adequacy
varieties.how: Time reversal: P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1. Factor reversal: P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = value ratio. Fisher passes both; only fixed-weight and GM indices pass the circular test.

example.q: An index satisfies P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1. Which test is this?
steps: P₁₀ is the index computed backwards, from year 1 to year 0.
An index that gives consistent results forwards and backwards passes the time reversal test.

varieties.name: Link relatives and chain index
varieties.how: Link relative = this year ÷ last year × 100. Chain index = link relative × previous chain index ÷ 100.

example.q: Link relatives for years 2, 3 and 4 are 110, 120 and 90 (year 1 = 100). Find the chain-base indices.

varieties.name: Base shifting and splicing
varieties.how: Divide every index by the index of the new base year and multiply by 100.

example.q: On base 2018 = 100, the index is 125 in 2020 and 150 in 2023. Find the 2023 index on base 2020 = 100.
steps: New index = old index ÷ old index of the new base × 100.

varieties.name: Cost of living index and real wages
varieties.how: Family budget method: CLI = ΣIW ÷ ΣW. Real wage = money wage ÷ CLI × 100.

example.q: Group weights and indices: food 50 and 120, rent 20 and 150, others 30 and 110. Find the cost of living index.

tips: Laspeyres = base quantities (L for "last", the old year). Paasche = present quantities.
Fisher = √(L × P). It is the only common formula passing both time reversal and factor reversal, hence "ideal".
Base shifting is a single division: new = old ÷ old value of new base × 100.
Real wage = money wage × 100 ÷ CPI. To keep the real wage the same, the money wage must rise by the same percentage as the CPI.
The family budget method and the aggregate expenditure method give the same cost of living index.
Chain index for one item equals the fixed-base index; for many items they can differ.
traps: In Laspeyres both numerator and denominator use q₀; in Paasche both use q₁. Do not mix them.
Time reversal is checked without the factor 100: P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1, not 100.
Fisher does not satisfy the circular test.
A fall in the index (say 125 to 100) is a 20% fall, not 25%; percentage change uses the earlier index as base.
The simple aggregative index fails the unit test: changing kg to quintal changes the answer.

questions.q: The index number for the base year is always:
questions.solution: The base period is the point of comparison, so its index is taken as 100.

questions.q: The sum of prices of a group of goods is ₹120 in the base year and ₹150 in the current year. The simple aggregative price index is:
Which index number satisfies both the time reversal test and the factor reversal test?
questions.solution: Fisher's ideal index √(L × P) satisfies both the time reversal and factor reversal tests. Laspeyres and Paasche satisfy neither.
